title: A third-party API is slow. How do you protect your service?
description: Timeouts, caching, hedging, degradation, and decoupling: making an unreliable dependency a bounded part of your latency budget.

data.text: **Question:** A third-party API is slow. How do you protect your service?

Bound the damage first: a **tight timeout** (the dependency can never consume more than its slice of your latency budget), **retry only idempotent calls** with backoff, a **circuit breaker** so a dead vendor fails fast instead of tying up threads, and a **cached or degraded fallback** so users still get something (last-known rates, placeholder data, queued processing). Then reduce exposure: **batch and prefetch** vendor calls instead of per-request fan-out, **decouple asynchronously** (queue the integration — the user doesn't wait for the vendor), and if the vendor is on a critical sync path, negotiate SLAs or evaluate alternatives. Measure per-dependency latency (tracing spans) so the vendor's contribution to your p99 is visible.

items: Budget math: if your p99 target is 500ms and the vendor's p99 is 800ms, no amount of tuning fixes it — move them off the sync path
Timeouts per attempt, sized to the budget (e.g., 300ms), not the default infinite HttpClient timeout
Retries: only if idempotent (GET, or POST with Idempotency-Key); 1–2 attempts max on a user-facing path
Circuit breaker: after N timeouts/5xx, fail fast for 30s; serve fallback while open
Fallbacks: cache last successful response (with staleness the business accepts), default values, or 'we'll process this shortly' async acknowledgment
Hedging (advanced): fire a second call after p95 of the first — lowers tail latency at the cost of duplicate vendor load; only with idempotency
Batching/prefetch: one call for 50 rows beats 50 calls; background refresh keeps caches warm
Async decoupling: publish 'ChargeRequested' to a queue; the vendor call happens in a worker with its own retry/DLQ — user gets instant acknowledgment
Vendor-side facts: ask for their p99/SLA, connection reuse, regional endpoints; DNS/TLS setup overhead often dominates short calls

data.title: Bounded vendor call with cache fallback in .NET

items: Default (100s) HttpClient timeout — one hung vendor pins your worker threads
Retrying non-idempotent vendor POSTs — duplicate charges on their side
No per-dependency tracing — the vendor's share of your p99 is invisible
Blocking the user response on a vendor that isn't needed for that response
Serving stale cache with no staleness bound or logging — silent data rot
One shared circuit-breaker policy for all vendors — the slow one shouldn't trip the fast one's budget

When is a hedged request worth the duplicate load?
How do you keep a queue-fed vendor integration observable?
How would you prove to the business that async processing is acceptable here?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Timeout → bounded retries → breaker → cache/degraded fallback, in that order
The vendor's latency budget must fit inside yours, or they leave the sync path
Batch/prefetch; decouple with queues when the answer isn't needed immediately
Per-dependency tracing makes the vendor's p99 contribution visible
data.takeaway: You can't make a third party faster — you can only make their worst day a bounded, visible, survivable slice of yours.
